html:
The spread of Greek cities around the Mediterranean and the Black Sea between about 750 and 550 BCE. Cities of the Greek mainland and Ionia sent out groups of settlers to found new, self-governing cities, driven by a lack of land, by trade or by strife at home.

The main areas were:

  • southern Italy and Sicily, so thick with colonies it was called Magna Graecia, with Syracuse, founded by Corinth, the greatest;
  • the northern Aegean and the straits, where Megara founded Byzantium;
  • the Black Sea coasts, a source of grain, fish and slaves;
  • the far west, with Massalia (Marseille) in southern France, and Cyrene in Libya.

Greek colonists met Phoenician traders, who planted their own colonies such as Carthage and Gadir, and Etruscans, Scythians and others. They spread the Greek language, the olive and the vine, coins, and the alphabet, which passed on to the Etruscans and the Romans.
